query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles, the onset of premelting is driven by a localized surface segregation of the lower‐melting constituents (especially Cu) that create liquid‐like domains at the nanoparticle periphery. These domains then coalesce via a percolative mechanism as temperature rises, effectively lowering the overall melting onset compared to a compositionally uniform solid solution.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles synthesized as single-phase solid solutions with an initially uniform elemental distribution among Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu.
generation.intervention: Controlled heating experiments with in situ imaging (e.g., neutron imaging or TEM heating) comparing nanoparticles prepared under conditions that maintain compositional homogeneity versus those pretreated to induce slight surface segregation.
generation.conditions: Heating across the premelting to melting regime under inert atmosphere with controlled (slow) heating rates; applicable for nanoparticle sizes in the tens-of-nanometer range where surface effects dominate.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of compositionally enriched surface layers (domains enriched in Cu and possibly other lower-melting elements) which act as nucleation sites for liquid formation.
generation.mechanism: Differential melting temperatures of individual elements lead to local vibrational and diffusive processes that promote surface segregation. Once regions enriched in low‐melting constituents form at the surface, premelting starts locally and propagates by merging these liquid regions, thus reducing the apparent melting onset temperature of the entire nanoparticle.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline nanoparticle with a more uniform elemental distribution, nanoparticles exhibiting surface compositional modulation will show early (premelting) formation of liquid domains at the periphery (detectable as localized shape changes or radiographic contrast variations) at temperatures several tens of degrees below the bulk melting point.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy nanoparticles that remain compositionally homogeneous during heating, showing a relatively sharp and simultaneous bulk melting transition.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoparticles in which the size (typically tens of nm) makes surface effects significant and for multicomponent alloys where the constituent elements have distinctly different melting points. It may not apply if the nanoparticle size increases substantially (minimizing surface-to-volume ratio) or if extreme cooling/heating rates entirely suppress diffusive segregation.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from in situ neutron imaging of molten HEAs (PMC8320920) and atomic simulations indicating grain-boundary or interface‐premelting in related high-entropy systems (PMC6479918) support a role for local compositional effects, directly linking localized surface segregation to a percolative premelting mechanism in a chemically complex Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu system is an extrapolation. The quantitative extent of segregation and its effect on the melting onset remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform controlled in situ heating experiments on Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles using a high-resolution imaging technique (such as cold neutron imaging or TEM heating) to monitor the evolution of surface composition and morphology. Prepare two sets: one set where processing minimizes elemental segregation, and a second set intentionally preconditioned to promote slight surface segregation. Compare the temperature at which liquid-like domains first appear at the surface.
measurements: Real-time imaging of shape and intensity changes (indicating liquid formation) at the nanoparticle surface.
Elemental maps (via EDX or similar) during heating to detect enrichment of low-melting components.
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) profiles to determine onset temperatures for melting.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no detectable difference in the early onset of surface melting (i.e., no localized liquid formation at the periphery observed below the melting onset of homogeneous particles) is seen between nanoparticles with and without induced segregation, or if the melting transition occurs uniformly without any evidence of a percolative liquid network, then the hypothesis that localized surface segregation governs premelting would be falsified.
